n: The second part of Zechariah (chapters 9–14) looks further ahead, especially to the Messiah. It opens with judgment on Israel’s northern neighbors in Syria — everyone, Israel included, will look to the Lord.

f.g: A region in northern Syria, known from Assyrian records.

n: Hamath, also in Syria, and the proud Phoenician cities of Tyre and Sidon, famous for their cleverness, are included.
Tyre built itself an island fortress and piled up silver and gold like dust and mud. Wealth bred false security.

f.g: Tyre was an island city with massive walls — a pun, since “stronghold” (matsor) sounds like “Tyre” (Tsor).

n: But the Lord will strip Tyre, destroy its sea power, and burn it. Alexander the Great famously captured island Tyre in 332 BC.

f.w: she shall be devoured with fire

n: The Philistine cities — Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron — will watch Tyre fall and tremble, for their hopes will be dashed.

f.g: What they relied on (Tyre) will fail them.

n: Foreigners of mixed descent will live in Ashdod, and Philistine pride will be cut off.

f.g: A mixed or foreign people — Ashdod’s native population would be replaced.

n: God will remove the bloody, unclean food from Philistia’s mouth, and a remnant will belong to God, absorbed into Judah like the Jebusites of Jerusalem. Even enemies can be converted.

f.w: his abominations from between his teeth

n: God will camp around His house like a guard, so no oppressor will overrun His people again. He is watching.

f.w: I will encamp about mine house

n: A famous messianic prophecy: Zion’s King comes righteous and bringing salvation, humble and riding on a donkey’s colt. Jesus fulfilled this at His triumphal entry into Jerusalem.

f.w: behold, thy King cometh unto thee

f.g: A donkey, the mount of peace, rather than a warhorse — fitting for the Prince of Peace.

n: This King will end war, removing chariots, warhorses, and bows. He will speak peace to the nations and rule from sea to sea, to the ends of the earth.

f.w: he shall speak peace unto the heathen

n: Because of the blood of the covenant, God frees prisoners from a waterless pit. Jesus spoke of His “blood of the new testament [covenant]” at the Last Supper.

f.w: the pit wherein is no water

n: Return to the stronghold, “prisoners of hope”! God promises to restore double what was lost.

f.g: Captives who hold onto hope — a beautiful phrase for God’s people in trial.

f.w: I will render double unto thee

n: God will use Judah and Ephraim as His bow and arrow against Greece. Many see here the later Jewish struggles against Greek rulers (the Maccabees, about 167 BC).
The Lord will appear over His people; His arrows will flash like lightning. He will sound the trumpet and march in the southern storms.

f.w: his arrow shall go forth as the lightning

n: The Lord will defend them. They will triumph and celebrate noisily, filled like the sacrificial bowls that caught blood at the altar’s corners.
On that day God will save His people like a shepherd saves his flock. They will sparkle like jewels in a crown on His land.

f.w: as the flock of his people

n: How good and beautiful He is! Grain and new wine will make young men and women flourish — a picture of abundant blessing.
